description: A four-panel composite figure of combined true tensile stress–strain and work-hardening-rate curves for Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels. All panels share identical axes: x = ε_T, True tensile strain (labelled 0.0–0.8); y = σ_T & Θ (SS and WH), MPa (labelled 0, 1000, 2000, 3000). In every panel solid lines are the true tensile stress–strain (SS) curves and dashed lines the work hardening (WH) rate curves, each with a matching colour-coded legend in the upper right. (a) effect of C content after solution treatment at 1050 °C, legend: 0.6C (black), 1.0C (red), 1.2C (green), 1.5C (blue). (b) effect of Mn at 1050 °C, legend: 20Mn, 25Mn, 30Mn, 35Mn (black, red, green, blue). (c) effect of Al at 1050 °C and (d) effect of Al at 1100 °C, both with legend 6Al, 8Al, 10Al, 11Al, 12Al (black, red, green, blue, cyan). The solid SS curves of all conditions rise almost linearly and terminate at similar peak true stresses (between the 1000 and 2000 MPa gridlines), whereas the dashed WH curves separate widely, descending from near 3000 MPa at very low strain. WH-rate ranking: higher for 0.6C, for 35Mn, and for 6Al; lower for high C, low Mn and high Al. Panel (d) reproduces the Al ordering after the 1100 °C treatment, with the solid curves reaching larger true strain. Together the panels argue that alloying content changes work-hardening capacity rather than the peak flow stress.

subfigures.description: True stress-strain and work hardening rate curves showing the effect of C content (0.6C black, 1.0C red, 1.2C green, 1.5C blue) after solution treatment at 1050 °C; the black 0.6C dashed WH curve is the highest and declines monotonically from near 3000 MPa at low strain, while the other dashed curves show an initial drop, a slow rise and a second drop.

Same curve pair format for the effect of Mn content (20Mn black, 25Mn red, 30Mn green, 35Mn blue) after 1050 °C solution treatment; the blue 35Mn dashed WH curve is highest (plateau near the 2000 MPa gridline) and the green 30Mn curve decreases monotonically, while the black 20Mn WH curve is lowest.

Same format for the effect of Al content (6Al black, 8Al red, 10Al green, 11Al blue, 12Al cyan) after 1050 °C; the black 6Al dashed WH curve is highest (plateau around the 2000 MPa gridline) and the cyan 12Al curve among the lowest, i.e. WH rate falls as Al increases.

Same five Al labels (6Al–12Al, same colours) but after solution treatment at 1100 °C; the dashed WH curves retain the ordering 6Al highest to 12Al lowest, and the solid stress-strain curves extend to noticeably larger true strain (some terminating beyond 0.5) than in panel (c).

observations.observation: Every panel plots two curve families on identical axes: ε_T, True tensile strain (0.0–0.8) versus σ_T & Θ (SS and WH) in MPa (0–3000), with solid lines for true stress-strain and dashed lines for work hardening rate.

In panel (a) the dashed work hardening rate curves are ranked with the black 0.6C curve highest, reaching the top 3000 MPa gridline at very low strain, and the WH rate decreasing as C content increases to 1.5C (blue).

In panel (b) the dashed work hardening rate curves increase with Mn content; the blue 35Mn curve is highest (plateau near the 2000 MPa gridline) and the black 20Mn curve is lowest, the reverse ranking of panel (a).

In panels (c) and (d) the dashed work hardening rate curves decrease with increasing Al: the black 6Al curve is highest, the cyan 12Al among the lowest, and this ordering is preserved at both 1050 °C (c) and 1100 °C (d).

The black dashed 0.6C curve of (a) and the green dashed 30Mn curve of (b) fall monotonically from a sharp low-strain maximum, whereas the remaining dashed curves decline rapidly, rise slowly, then decline again.
All solid stress-strain curves, regardless of C, Mn or Al content, terminate at comparable peak true stresses lying between the 1000 and 2000 MPa gridlines (no numeric end-point labels are printed).
The caption states that solid lines are true tensile stress-strain (SS) curves and dashed lines are work hardening (WH) rate curves.

The caption states that (a) shows the effect of C content and (b) the effect of Mn content after solution treatment at 1050 °C, while (c) and (d) show the effect of Al content after solution treatment at 1050 °C and 1100 °C respectively.
The citing text states that σ_TS was estimated as about 1350 MPa for all the designed low-density steels and is not significantly affected by C, Mn and Al content.
The citing text states that σ_FS was estimated as about 2150 MPa for all investigated steels, implying fracture strength is also independent of alloying content and microstructure.
The citing text states a maximum work hardening rate of around 1900 MPa in the 0.6%C steel (Fig. 8a), around 2300 MPa in the 35%Mn steel (Fig. 8b), and around 2100 MPa for the 6%Al steel (Fig. 8c).
The citing text states that the work hardening rate increases with decreasing carbon content and with decreasing Al content, and increases with increasing Mn content.
The citing text attributes the lower work hardening rate to larger κ-carbide size, since shear deformation allows dislocations to glide across κ-carbide shear planes.
The citing text notes that high ductility is only generated in low-density steels with a high work hardening rate capacity.

unreadable_items: No numeric end-point labels are printed on any curve in panels (a)-(d), so peak true stress and peak work hardening rate values cannot be read from the pixels; values in the citing text are not printed on the figure.
The word 'alloved' in the caption is a typographical error for 'alloyed' (caption text, not figure content).
